title: Do trees share through fungi?
teaches: The two kinds of root fungi and what the evidence shows about carbon passing between trees
summary: **Most land plants partner with root fungi.** In this mycorrhiza the fungus gathers phosphorus, nitrogen and water from far more soil than roots reach, and the plant pays in sugar and fat.
**Root fungi come in two main kinds.** Arbuscular fungi grow inside the root cells of most plants, while sheath fungi wrap the root tips of forest trees and make many autumn mushrooms.
**One fungus can link many trees.** Mapping showed single fungi joining dozens of Douglas-firs in a stand.

**Tree-to-tree sharing through fungi is still debated.** Simard reported carbon passing from birch to fir in 1997, but a 2023 review found the field evidence thin and routes through soil not ruled out.

blocks.text: Walk through a birch wood in autumn and the fly agarics, red with white flecks, come up under the birches, and under pines and spruces, but not in the open meadow beside them. Under the beeches there are other mushrooms again. Some fungi seem tied to particular kinds of tree, as if they needed them.

Many of them do, though most partner more than one kind of tree. Each of those mushrooms is the fruit of a mycelium wrapped round the tree's fine roots. In the 1880s the German botanist Albert Bernhard Frank, asked by the Prussian government to find out how to grow truffles, found the roots of every oak, beech and pine he dug sheathed in fungus, and in 1885 called the pairing a **mycorrhiza**, Greek for fungus-root.[^frank] It turned out to be the rule rather than the exception. About nine in ten land plant species form mycorrhizas, from grasses and wheat to the tallest trees. There are several kinds, of which this lesson follows the two commonest; heathers and orchids have kinds of their own.

The partnership is a trade. A hypha is a fraction of the width of the finest root, so for the same cost in material a fungus can lay down hundreds of times more length, and reach soil the roots never touch. It gathers water, nitrogen, and above all phosphorus (which clings to soil grains and barely moves, so a root soon uses up what lies right beside it) and passes them to the plant. In return the plant passes sugar and fats to the fungus, a share of everything it makes by photosynthesis that has been estimated at up to a fifth.[^cost]

It is not charity on either side. In 2011 Toby Kiers and her colleagues grew a plant's roots with several arbuscular fungi at once, some generous with phosphorus and some stingy, and labelled the carbon the plant sent down with a rare, traceable form of carbon, so they could see which fungus received it. The plant sent more carbon to the fungi that gave more phosphorus, and the fungi sent more phosphorus to roots that gave more carbon. Each side rewards the partner that pays.

Root fungi come in two main kinds, which do it differently. **Arbuscular fungi** push into the root and through the walls of its cells, and inside each cell they branch into a tiny tree, the arbuscule, pressed against the cell's membrane, where the trading happens. They partner about seven in ten plant species, including most grasses, crops and tropical trees. They make no mushrooms at all; they live as threads in soil and roots and as large spores in the soil. They are among the oldest of all fungal partners: in the Rhynie chert of Scotland,[^rhynie] some of the first land plants have arbuscules in their stems, preserved in stone.

blocks.caption: The two main kinds of root fungus, each in a root cut lengthwise and magnified. Left: the fungus sheathes the root tip and threads a net between its outer cells. Right: the fungus enters the cells and branches into tiny trees.

blocks.text: **Sheath fungi**, or ectomycorrhizal fungi, stay outside the root's cells. They wrap each root tip in a felt of hyphae and thread a net between its outer cells.[^net] They partner fewer plant species, around one in fifty, but those include most of the trees of northern and mountain forests: pines, firs, spruces, oaks, beeches, birches, and the eucalypts of Australia. The sheath fungi evolved many separate times, mostly among club fungi, and they make many of the familiar mushrooms of the woods: boletes, chanterelles, fly agarics, and the truffles of lesson 6.

A sheath fungus is not tied to one tree. Its mycelium can wrap the roots of several at once, so that two trees share the same fungus. In 2010 Kevin Beiler and his colleagues in British Columbia mapped the fungi on the roots of every Douglas-fir in a small plot, using DNA to tell one individual fungus from another. Most trees were linked to others through at least one shared fungus. The best-connected tree, one of the oldest, was linked to 47 others.

Links like these raised the question of whether anything passes from tree to tree. In the 1990s Suzanne Simard, a forest researcher in British Columbia, planted paper birch and Douglas-fir seedlings side by side in the forest. She enclosed each seedling's leaves in a bag, so that each took in only the air she gave it, and fed the birch carbon dioxide carrying one rare form of carbon and the fir another, so that the carbon each one fixed could be traced.[^label] When she published the results in 1997, more labelled carbon had gone from birch to fir than the other way, and when the fir was shaded and made less sugar of its own, it received more. *Nature* featured the paper on its cover, using the phrase **wood wide web**, which soon stuck. Because the bags controlled only what went into the leaves, they could not show which way the carbon had travelled underground: through the fungus or through the soil.

blocks.caption: A model of a birch and fir labelling experiment in eight plots. Each dot is one pair of seedlings; the bar shows the range in which the true average very probably lies. A fine mesh between the seedlings stops fungal threads but lets water through, the control later studies used.
blocks.task: Shade the fir heavily, and put in the mesh

blocks.text: The idea spread far beyond the paper. Over the next twenty years it grew, in books, films and news stories, into forests where old mother trees (a popular name for the big old trees at the centre of the links) feed their seedlings and warn their neighbours of attack through a fungal internet. In 2023 Justine Karst, Melanie Jones and Jason Hoeksema went back to the field studies to see how much of that the evidence supported.

They found much less than the story claimed. Studies that had mapped shared fungi in the field were few, and covered only a handful of forest types. Studies that found carbon or nutrients moving between trees mostly found small amounts, scattered widely from plot to plot, as the model shows, and several found none. Few had ruled out the other routes: carbon leaking from one tree's roots into the soil and being taken up by the other, or travelling into a shared fungus and staying in the fungus's own threads inside the second tree's roots without entering the tree itself. And there was no field study showing that carbon passing through a fungus helped the tree that got it. They also checked how later papers cited the field studies, and found that a large share described them as showing more than they had found, such as transfer that helped seedlings survive.

Simard and others have answered that the critique overlooked results, and the argument goes on in the journals. What both sides accept is the core of this lesson: almost every plant trades with fungi, and in forests many trees share the same fungi. Whether trees use those shared fungi to help each other, and how much, is an open question being tested, plot by plot, with better controls.

blocks.caption: Five questions on root fungi
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: What does a plant get from its root fungus?
choices: Phosphorus, nitrogen and water from soil its roots cannot reach
items.why: Hyphae are far thinner and cheaper than roots, so the fungus explores much more soil and passes nutrients to the plant, which pays in sugar and fat.

items.ask: Which kind of root fungus branches into tiny trees inside the root's cells?
items.why: Arbuscular fungi enter the cells and form arbuscules. Sheath fungi stay outside the cells, wrapping the root tip.

items.ask: Why do fly agarics come up only under birches and pines?
choices: They are sheath fungi living on those trees' roots
They feed on fallen birch bark only
Birch and pine shade suits their spores
items.why: The mushroom is the fruit of a mycelium partnered with the tree's roots, so it appears where its partner trees grow.

choices: Labelled carbon passed from birch to fir, more so when the fir was shaded
Firs poisoned birches through the soil
No carbon passed between the seedlings
items.why: She fed each species a different labelled carbon and found more moving from birch to fir than back, with more going to shaded firs.

items.ask: Which of these did Karst and colleagues find in their 2023 review?
choices: Few studies had ruled out carbon moving through the soil instead of through fungi
Root fungi do not exist in forests
items.why: They accepted that trees share fungi, but found the evidence for transfer through those links thin, small and often open to other explanations.

frank.title: Frank and the truffles
frank.text: Frank never found a way to grow truffles, but in looking for them he found that the roots of the trees they grew under were wrapped in fungus, and argued, against the view that the fungi were parasites, that tree and fungus fed each other.

cost.title: What the fungus costs
cost.text: Estimates of the plant's carbon going to its fungi range widely, from a few per cent to around a fifth, depending on the plant, the fungus and how much phosphorus is in the soil. In rich soil, plants send their fungi less.

net.title: The Hartig net
net.text: The net of hyphae between a root's outer cells is named after the German forester Theodor Hartig, who drew it in 1842 without knowing it was a fungus. It is where the sheath fungus and the root trade.

label.title: Labelled carbon
label.text: Almost all carbon is carbon-12. Simard fed one tree carbon dioxide made with carbon-13, a rare stable form, and the other with carbon-14, a radioactive form, so that each tree's carbon could be measured in the other's tissues.

rhynie.title: The Rhynie chert
rhynie.text: Near the village of Rhynie in Aberdeenshire, hot springs full of dissolved silica flooded a marsh about 407 million years ago. The silica hardened into chert, a fine quartz rock, before the plants and fungi could rot, preserving them cell by cell.
